pr_title: GDScript: Do not warn about static call from inside a class
pr_body:
Do not warn about static call if it is done by identifier directly from inside a class. Test for no warning:
```gdscript
static func ok() -> void:
  print('OK')

func test():
  ok()
```

Currently Godot does complain and only solution to avoid that is to use `class_name` which pollutes global namespace. 

It is kinda strange actually that Godot allows access to static members through an instance: `instance.MyEnum`, `instance.MyConst` or `instance.InnerClass`. What other languages do support that?

Fixes #69282.
pr_comments:
Ok, I was told that there were discussions about this before and there were some opposition to disabling the warning for such case.

For record and in case the opposition is still strong - I can narrow down the exception for the warning even more:

a) To only user defined methods, so for Godot's built-in funcs that are inherited you will still have to call with a class. Which is ok because they already have a name and it makes clearer where a function comes from.

b) To only the same class that defines the function. Which is ok because it will be possible to store base class in a const so there will be no global pollution (but a small member one).

> It is kinda strange actually that Godot allows access to static members through an instance: `instance.MyEnum`, `instance.MyConst` or `instance.InnerClass`. What other languages do support that?

I'm under the impression most languages allow this. At least I know C++ and Python do.

Given this, I'm not sure why such warning exists in the first place. It was added in #67365 because of some confusion created by the conversion from 3.x to 4.x with the introduction of static methods for native types. I'm not sure this warning is a good solution to the issue though.

Hm, interesting, decided to check. 

Seems like this is old-school thing. C++, Java and Python do allow access to static things through an instance. But newer languages - C#, Kotlin, Scala, Ruby, TypeScript, Rust - do not (other languages just remove concept of static things completely).

Personally I am in favor of separation between class members and instance members.

But it shouldn't be done at expense of usability and global namespace pollution.
Well, I guess it makes sense to warn on this usage (calling static method from instance) but still allow it. In this case this PR should be merged.
In current form it will allow it, that's why I gave options for narrowing removal of warning in [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/70648#issuecomment-1367066772).

> In current form it will allow it, that's why I gave options for narrowing removal of warning in [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/70648#issuecomment-1367066772).

Thanks for confirming, either A and/or B sounds fine to me. @vnen what do you think?

BTW I am very glad you are looking into this. I implemented the warning, but I know nothing about GDScript so I was (and am) very lost when it comes to this stuff.

I believe the `b` to be somewhat annoying, since there isn't really a way to access the parent class without a name. Unless we make the `super` keyword work for this as well (although since this can access non-static methods as well, it could be confusing). So `a` is probably the best option.

> I believe the `b` to be somewhat annoying, since there isn't really a way to access the parent class without a name.

If I'm not mistaken, you can preload that unnamed class to a const.

After some time I realized that my real issue is that it is impossible to name (or refer) to current base class without making it global. Implementing such functionality is not hard and can be done in a few ways. The problem is not limited to calling static functions, another example - referring to a base class in typing annotations.

By going with exceptions for native static methods I'll introduce an inconsistency to the language. Which I would prefer to avoid.

So I'll close the PR. Sorry for those who gave thumbs up.

issue_context.title: Calling static function from within a class generates a warning
issue_context.body:
### Godot version

4.0.beta6

### System information

Windows 10

### Issue description

Hi all,

Calling a static function from within the class that owns it generates a warning. I would expect that calling the function from within the class shouldn't generate the warning (particularly if that class doesn't have a class name).

Thanks!

### Steps to reproduce

Add the below to a script and note the Error (warning) it generates:

```
func _ready() -> void:
    a_static_func()

static func a_static_func() -> void:
    pass
```

### Minimal reproduction project

N/A
comments:
This happens because ``_ready()`` is not a static function. As the warning indicates, you are calling a static function directly on an instance of the class (the current running instance of the script).

So, in this case the warning is _technically_ correct. But clearly it is annoying, and you are not the first person to think so. 

The reason we added this warning was mostly because many functions that you used to call on class instances in 3.x were made static. Instead of modifying an object, they return a new object. For example:
```
var tex = ImageTexture.new()
tex.create_from_image(some_img)
```
Is now written like:
```
var tex = ImageTexture.create_from_image(some_img)
```

The warning is useful here as it indicates to the user that ``tex.create_from_image()`` is not modifying the ``tex`` resource.

Additionally, from a code-quality standpoint, it is good practice to always call static functions from the class so that future readers of the code can distinguish between a function being called on an instance of a class or the class itself. 

However, the situation you point out above is a bit tricky. Since there is no specific class name, you have no choice but to just call the function directly. Even worse, the error message tells you to call the function on the class that your script inherits from. In other words, if your script looks like:
```
extends Control

func _ready() -> void:
    a_static_func()

static func a_static_func() -> void:
    pass
```

Then the warning tells you to use ``Control.a_static_func()`` which is not only annoying, but clearly wrong. 

I think we can carve out an exception to the warning, so it doesn't apply in this case. If not, we may just have to disable the warning whenever a static function is called from a method of the class it is defined in.

Thanks for the reply @clayjohn! 

I completely understand (and agree with) the purpose of the warning. From my perspective I think it makes sense to be able to call a static function from its class instance (particularly because some classes might not names as in your example). If you have a specific exception for unnamed classes then you create two different rules (and adding a class name later would mean refactoring any calls to it in the class). But I'll just follow Godot's lead! Haha.

This does beg a different question though: should I be naming more/all classes? I tend to limit it to things that need to be referenced elsewhere without a hierarchy relationship. Is the future of Godot every class being named? Or is my current philosophy correct?

To give some reference, in C# the code will not compile if you access a static method with `instance.StaticMethod()`. But it will compile happily if you call `StaticMethod` from a non-static method of `instance`. Which in turn will not compile if you write `this.StaticMethod()`. https://ideone.com/rLmBHF

review_comments: This doesn't permit the use of the`self` identifier.

Like was mentioned [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/69282#issuecomment-1329962963), in other languages (in the comment it is C#) it is allowed to call static functions just by identifier from inside a class, but not allowed to do so by calling `instance.stat()` or `this.stat()`. If the intention is to be like other languages then makes sense to keep the warning for `self.stat()`.
